title: hosted api tls session resumption latency spike postmortem
content:
Summary:

On 2026-06-21 between ~11:12 and 12:03 UTC we observed repeated regional latency spikes and elevated streaming tail latencies for the Hosted API (primarily us-west-2 and eu-west-1). Error rates (5xx) did not exceed typical background levels, but median and P95 streaming latencies increased by ~2–4x during several 3–8 minute windows. The user-facing impact: degraded interactive streaming experiences for ~7% of active connections in the affected regions and increased token delivery jitter for customers using long-lived SSE/websocket sessions.

Impact: 
- Client-visible streaming latency spikes and token delivery jitter for subset of sessions (~7% of active streaming connections).
- No broad request failures; most HTTP/gRPC non-streaming requests continued to succeed with increased response times in some cases.
- No data loss or model inference regressions observed.

Detection and timeline (all UTC):
- 2026-06-21 11:05 — SRE alerting: Streaming P95 latency for hosted-api-stream-route crossed the auto-alarms threshold. Pager triggered.
- 11:12 — Oncall (Evan) starts triage; initial dashboards show clustered P95 spikes correlated with specific edge nodes and a subset of TCP connections with unusually long TLS handshake durations.
- 11:18 — Engineering (edge-proxy) joined to analyze TLS traces. Client connection duration histograms show many connections with repeated full TLS handshakes instead of expected session resumption.
- 11:27 — Mitigation: temporarily increased edge-proxy connection keepalive timeout from 30s to 90s as a fast-patch to reduce churn and handshake rate; observed immediate reduction in new full-handshake counts.
- 11:40 — Partial rollback of a recent ALB configuration that had changed TLS session ticket lifetime (rolled out earlier that morning) — rollback confirmed; handshake rate fell further.
- 11:55 — Traffic and latency returned near baseline; monitoring continued for drift.
- 12:03 — Incident declared resolved; post-incident notes and runbook updates drafted.

Root cause analysis: 
Primary cause: configuration mismatch between the edge load balancer (managed ALB layer) TLS session ticket lifetime and upstream edge-proxy TLS session cache behavior. A morning change to the ALB TLS session ticket configuration reduced ticket validity from 24h to 60s (intended to speed key rotation for a different service). That change had unintended side-effects for long-lived streaming sessions proxied through our edge: the ALB began discarding session tickets aggressively, causing downstream clients/edge-proxy to perform full TLS handshakes frequently.

Secondary contributing factors: 
- edge-proxy connection pooling and ephemeral worker recycling policy was tuned to favor short lived connections (30s keepalive) for footprint efficiency; combined with frequent full handshakes this caused CPUs on some edge nodes to spike and created head-of-line scheduling on streaming worker threads.
- Insufficient alerting specificity: we had a generic spike alarm on streaming latency but no dedicated metric tracking TLS handshake type (full vs resumed) at edge node granularity before this incident.
- Recent ALB config change was made by platform infra as a safe default for other services; change happened during a non-peak maintenance window but lacked an SLO impact review for Streaming routes.

Why this caused the observed symptoms: 
Frequent full TLS handshakes increase per-connection CPU and I/O work on edge nodes. For long-lived streaming connections (SSE/websocket), token-by-token flushing depends on available worker thread scheduling and network send buffers. When CPU and scheduling pressure increased due to handshakes, token delivery experienced higher tail latency and intermittent bursts of delays, observable as jitter and P95 latency spikes without necessarily producing 5xx errors.

Mitigations taken during incident: 
- Increased edge-proxy keepalive to 90s to reduce connection churn and handshake rate (11:27). This gave immediate reduction in new handshake events.
- Rolled back the ALB TLS ticket lifetime change (11:40) to the previous 24h setting. This reduced failed resumption and eliminated the surge in full handshakes.
- Added temporary rate-limiting on TLS handshake acceptance per-worker as a defensive stopgap for nodes approaching CPU saturation. This was removed once baseline restored.

Post-incident recovery verification: 
- Monitored TLS full-handshake counts dropped to baseline within ~10 minutes of ALB rollback.
- Streaming P95 and tail-latency returned to baseline within ~15–20 minutes.
- No regression in throughput for non-streaming endpoints.

Longer-term action items (owners and ETA): 
1) Add TLS handshake/resumption telemetry to edge dashboards (metrics: full_handshakes, resumed_handshakes per-edge-node, session_ticket_misses). Owner: Priya Nair. ETA: 2026-07-05.
2) Add pre-deploy risk checklist item: any TLS/session ticket lifetime changes in ALBs must trigger an SRE impact review when there are streaming routes present. Owner: Jared Liu (platform). ETA: 2026-06-30.
3) Update edge-proxy default keepalive to 90s for streaming route pools; make it configurable per-route. Owner: Marta Gomez. ETA: 2026-07-07.
4) Implement a canary check in CI for edge config changes that simulates session-resumption behavior with long-lived streaming sessions. Owner: Edge infra team. ETA: 2026-07-20.
5) Run a capacity/stress test for TLS handshake storms on staging (to validate rate-limiting knobs and CPU headroom). Owner: eng-sre. ETA: 2026-07-15.
6) Create runbook playbook entries for TLS ticket/config-related incidents (detection, quick Mitigations, rollback checklist). Owner: Evan Morales. ETA: 2026-06-30.

Runbook/On-call notes (draft): 
- Detection signals: sudden rise in streaming P95 without corresponding 5xx spike, increased CPU on a subset of edge nodes, increased count of full TLS handshakes per second.
- Triage steps: check edge-node TLS metrics, correlate with ALB config changes (ticket lifetime, TLS versions), examine recent deploys/ALB changes in platform infra.
- Quick mitigation checklist: 1) increase edge-proxy keepalive (reduces churn), 2) apply temporary handshake rate-limiting per worker, 3) rollback ALB session-ticket lifetime or disable aggressive rotation for the route, 4) if necessary, divert streaming traffic to warm standby nodes (regional failover).
- Post-incident: schedule follow-up with platform infra to coordinate TLS setting changes; tag the change as "SRE-impact" in the change log.

Notable open questions: 
- Why was the ALB TLS ticket lifetime change applied without SRE notification? (platform process gap)
- Would longer term use of TLS 1.3 with stateless session resumption reduce risk here, and what is the compatibility matrix across our customers?

Communications: 
- Customer-facing note prepared for affected customers explaining transient streaming degradation and that no data or model outputs were lost. Drafted by Customer Success (CS lead: Ana Wallace); scheduled send 2026-06-24.
- Internal blameless postmortem review scheduled for 2026-06-29 16:00 UTC (invite: eng-sre, edge infra, platform infra, customer success).

Appendix (observability links & quick artifacts): 
- Streaming latency dashboard: https://metrics.redwood.ai/d/streaming/hosted-api-latency
- Edge TLS metric panel: https://metrics.redwood.ai/d/tls/edge-handshakes
- Incident ticket: INC-2026-1687 (https://jira.redwood.ai/browse/INC-2026-1687)
- Edge proxy PR for temporary keepalive tweak: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/412

Notes to self (oncall): 
- We should treat ALB session ticket lifetime as a cross-team config that requires SRE sign-off when streaming routes exist.
- Add a simple synthetic that opens long-lived streaming sessions and verifies resumed-handshake ratio daily in staging.

Status: draft. Will update after the blameless review and as action items progress.
